source: A frame of three beams
videos.handover: Try it: take three sticks of different lengths and see how many different triangles you can make, and what happens when two sticks are laid end to end along the third.
videos.note: The hook leaves the question open: do not say that a triangle cannot be built, and do not say how long the beams are. The compass construction and the triangle inequality settle it later.

source: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4

items.question: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm, and explain why AC and BC are both 4 cm.
steps: Draw the base AB of length 4 cm.
Step 1: with the compass set to 4 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
Step 2: keep the compass at 4 cm, put the point on B, and draw a second arc that crosses the first.
Mark the crossing point C. It is on the arc from A, so AC = 4 cm, and on the arc from B, so BC = 4 cm.
Step 3: join AC and BC. All three sides are 4 cm.
items.answer: An equilateral triangle ABC with AB = BC = CA = 4 cm

videos.answer: An equilateral triangle ABC with AB = BC = CA = 4 cm

source: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.

items.question: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
steps: Step 1: draw the base AB = 4 cm.
Step 2: with the compass set to 5 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
Step 3: set the compass to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc.
Step 4: the crossing point is C. It is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B. Join AC and BC.
Check with the ruler: AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
items.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm

videos.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm

source: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm an

items.question: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm and say what kind of triangle it is.
steps: Take the side of 6 cm as the base AB.
From A draw an arc of radius 4 cm, and from B draw an arc of radius 4 cm. They cross at C.
C is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B, so AC = BC = 4 cm.
Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.
items.answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm

videos.answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm

source: Construct (triangles from three sides)

items.question: Construct triangles having the following sidelengths (all the units are in cm): (a) 4, 4, 6 (b) 3, 4, 5 (c) 1, 5, 5 (d) 4, 6, 8 (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5. Say what kind of triangle each is.
steps: Each set satisfies the check: the two shorter lengths add to more than the longest (4 + 4 > 6, 3 + 4 > 5, 1 + 5 > 5, 4 + 6 > 8, 3.5 + 3.5 > 3.5), so each triangle can be built.
For each set draw the longest side as the base, then an arc of one of the other lengths from each end.
(a) 4, 4, 6 has two equal sides: isosceles. (b) 3, 4, 5 has three different sides: scalene. (c) 1, 5, 5 has two equal sides: isosceles, with a very short base.
(d) 4, 6, 8 has three different sides: scalene. (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5 has three equal sides: equilateral.
items.answer: All five can be built: (a) isosceles, (b) scalene, (c) isosceles, (d) scalene, (e) equilateral

videos.answer: All five can be built: (a) isosceles, (b) scalene, (c) isosceles, (d) scalene, (e) equilateral

source: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q1

items.question: A circle is drawn with its centre marked, and some points are marked on the circle. Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles.
steps: Mark the centre O and two points P and Q on the circle. Join OP, OQ and PQ.
OP and OQ are both radii of the same circle, so OP = OQ and triangle OPQ is isosceles.
Choosing P and Q so that PQ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take P and Q, then take R halfway between them on the circle, so that RP = RQ.
items.answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

videos.answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

source: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q2

items.question: Two circles of the same size have centres A and B, and each circle passes through the centre of the other. Then three circles of the same size have centres A, B and C, and each circle passes through the centres of the other two. Use the points on the circles and/or their centres to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.
steps: Two circles: each passes through the other's centre, so the radius equals AB. Let C and D be the two points where the circles cross.
C is on the circle at A, so AC = AB, and on the circle at B, so BC = AB. All three sides of triangle ABC are equal: it is equilateral. In the same way triangle ABD is equilateral.
AC = AD because both are radii of the circle at A, so triangle ACD is isosceles; triangle BCD is isosceles in the same way.

Three circles: A, B and C are the centres and every pair of centres is one radius apart, so triangle ABC is equilateral. Each pair of circles crosses in two points, and each crossing point together with those two centres gives another equilateral triangle.
Any point on a circle with the centre and another point on the same circle gives an isosceles triangle, as in the single circle.
items.answer: Triangles ABC and ABD are equilateral, and ACD and BCD are isosceles; with three circles ABC is equilateral and each crossing point forms more equilateral triangles

videos.answer: Triangles ABC and ABD are equilateral, and ACD and BCD are isosceles; with three circles ABC is equilateral and each crossing point forms more equilateral triangles

source: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and

items.question: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm, and say what happens to the arcs.
steps: Take 8 cm as the base AB. Draw an arc of 3 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B.
The arc from A reaches 3 cm along the base and the arc from B reaches 4 cm back, which covers 3 + 4 = 7 cm of the 8 cm. They do not meet.
For 2, 3 and 6, take 6 cm as the base. The arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm cover 2 + 3 = 5 cm of the 6 cm and do not meet.
In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6.
items.answer: No triangle can be built for 3, 4, 8 or for 2, 3, 6: the arcs never meet

videos.answer: No triangle can be built for 3, 4, 8 or for 2, 3, 6: the arcs never meet

source: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. T

items.question: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
steps: Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
items.answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

videos.answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

source: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 c

items.question: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm? Compare each direct length with the roundabout length.
steps: Between B and C: direct BC = 10 cm; roundabout BA + AC = 15 + 30 = 45 cm. 10 < 45, which is fine.
Between A and B: direct AB = 15 cm; roundabout AC + CB = 30 + 10 = 40 cm. 15 < 40, which is fine.
Between C and A: direct CA = 30 cm; roundabout CB + BA = 10 + 15 = 25 cm. 30 > 25, which is absurd.
One direct path is longer than its roundabout path, so no triangle exists.
items.answer: No triangle exists: 30 is greater than 10 + 15 = 25

videos.answer: No triangle exists: 30 is greater than 10 + 15 = 25

source: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having

items.question: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm? Verify by construction.
steps: The longest length is 7 cm. The other two add to 3 + 3 = 6 cm.
7 > 6, so the direct path of 7 cm is longer than the roundabout path of 6 cm. No triangle exists.
Check by construction: take the 7 cm side as the base and draw an arc of 3 cm from each end. The arcs cover 6 cm of the 7 cm and do not meet.
Rearranging the lengths does not help: 7 is still more than 3 + 3.
items.answer: No triangle exists for 3, 3 and 7

videos.answer: No triangle exists for 3, 3 and 7

source: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q1

items.question: We checked by construction that there are no triangles having sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm; and 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm. Check if you could have found this without trying to construct the triangle.
steps: For 3, 4 and 8: the longest is 8 and the other two add to 3 + 4 = 7.
8 > 7, so the direct length is longer than the roundabout length: no triangle.
For 2, 3 and 6: the longest is 6 and the other two add to 2 + 3 = 5.
6 > 5, so again no triangle. No construction was needed.
items.answer: Yes: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6, so neither set makes a triangle

videos.answer: Yes: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6, so neither set makes a triangle

source: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q2

items.question: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle for each of the following sets of lengths? (a) 10 km, 10 km and 25 km (b) 5 mm, 10 mm and 20 mm (c) 12 cm, 20 cm and 40 cm
steps: Compare the longest length with the sum of the other two; all three lengths in a set have the same unit.
(a) 10 + 10 = 20 and 20 < 25: no triangle.
(b) 5 + 10 = 15 and 15 < 20: no triangle.
(c) 12 + 20 = 32 and 32 < 40: no triangle.
items.answer: No triangle exists in any of the three sets: (a) 20 < 25, (b) 15 < 20, (c) 32 < 40

videos.answer: No triangle exists in any of the three sets: (a) 20 < 25, (b) 15 < 20, (c) 32 < 40

source: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q3 (Try This)

items.question: For the set 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm, two comparisons hold (10 < 15 + 30 and 15 < 10 + 30) but the third does not (30 > 10 + 15). Will there always be at least two comparisons where the direct length is less than the sum of the other two? Explore for different sets of lengths. Is it possible to tell which lengths will immediately be less than the sum of the other two, without calculations? [Hint: Consider the lengths in increasing order.]
steps: Write the lengths in increasing order: a, b, c with a ≤ b ≤ c.
The length c is the longest, so a < b + c is true because b + c is already at least c, which is at least a. Also b < a + c, because a + c is at least c, which is at least b.
Only the comparison for c, c < a + b, can fail.
Test with 7, 10, 15: 7 < 10 + 15 = 25 and 10 < 7 + 15 = 22 hold, and the longest check 15 < 7 + 10 = 17 holds too. For 10, 15, 30 the first two hold and only the longest check, 30 < 25, fails.
So at least two comparisons always hold, and the two that always hold belong to the two shorter lengths. Only the longest length needs a check.
items.answer: Yes, at least two comparisons always hold: the two shorter lengths are always less than the sum of the other two, so only the longest length needs to be checked

videos.answer: Yes, at least two comparisons always hold: the two shorter lengths are always less than the sum of the other two, so only the longest length needs to be checked

source: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm?

items.question: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm? Picture the circles on the longest side.
steps: Check the longest length: 8 < 4 + 5 = 9, so the triangle inequality is satisfied.
Take the base AB = 8 cm. Draw a circle of radius 4 cm at A and a circle of radius 5 cm at B.
Let X be the point where the circle at A meets AB. Then AX = 4 cm, so BX = 8 − 4 = 4 cm.
BX = 4 cm is less than the radius 5 cm of the circle at B, so the circle at B goes beyond X, into the circle at A. The circles cross at two points.
Either crossing point with A and B gives a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm.
items.answer: Yes, a triangle exists with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm: the two circles cross at two points

videos.answer: Yes, a triangle exists with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm: the two circles cross at two points

source: Check the lengths 6, 7 and 12 by comparing only the longest

items.question: Check the lengths 6, 7 and 12 by comparing only the longest length with the sum of the other two, and then check the other two comparisons to see that they hold.
steps: The longest length is 12. The other two add to 6 + 7 = 13.
12 < 13, so the longest comparison holds.
The other two comparisons: 6 < 7 + 12 = 19 and 7 < 6 + 12 = 18. Both hold, as they must, because 12 is already bigger than 6 and than 7.
All three hold, so the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality.
items.answer: The lengths 6, 7 and 12 satisfy the triangle inequality: 12 < 13 is the only check needed

videos.answer: The lengths 6, 7 and 12 satisfy the triangle inequality: 12 < 13 is the only check needed

source: Figure it Out (which lengths make a triangle), Q1

items.question: Which of the following lengths can be the sidelengths of a triangle? Explain your answers. Note that for each set, the three lengths have the same unit of measure. (a) 2, 2, 5 (b) 3, 4, 6 (c) 2, 4, 8 (d) 5, 5, 8 (e) 10, 20, 25 (f) 10, 20, 35 (g) 24, 26, 28
steps: Compare the longest length with the sum of the other two.
(a) 2 + 2 = 4 < 5: no triangle. (b) 3 + 4 = 7 > 6: a triangle. (c) 2 + 4 = 6 < 8: no triangle.
(d) 5 + 5 = 10 > 8: a triangle. (e) 10 + 20 = 30 > 25: a triangle. (f) 10 + 20 = 30 < 35: no triangle.
(g) 24 + 26 = 50 > 28: a triangle.
items.answer: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)

videos.answer: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)

source: On a base AB, take two circles whose radii are the two small

items.question: On a base AB, take two circles whose radii are the two smaller lengths. For the sets 3, 5, 8 and 2, 5, 8 and 5, 6, 8 say whether the circles touch, miss or cross, and whether a triangle exists.
steps: 3, 5, 8: the base is 8 and the radii are 3 and 5. The radii add to 3 + 5 = 8, equal to the base, so the circles touch at one point. No triangle.
2, 5, 8: the radii add to 2 + 5 = 7, less than 8, so the circles miss. No triangle.
5, 6, 8: the radii add to 5 + 6 = 11, more than 8, so the circles cross in two points. A triangle exists.
items.answer: 3, 5, 8: touch, no triangle; 2, 5, 8: miss, no triangle; 5, 6, 8: cross, a triangle exists

videos.answer: 3, 5, 8: touch, no triangle; 2, 5, 8: miss, no triangle; 5, 6, 8: cross, a triangle exists

source: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths ca

items.question: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths can make a triangle, and use it on 3.5, 6 and 9, and on 4, 7 and 11.
steps: Step 1: find the longest length.
Step 2: add the other two lengths.
Step 3: if the sum is more than the longest, a triangle exists; if the sum is equal or less, it does not.
3.5, 6, 9: the longest is 9 and 3.5 + 6 = 9.5. 9.5 > 9, so a triangle exists.
4, 7, 11: the longest is 11 and 4 + 7 = 11. The sum equals the longest, so the circles touch and no triangle exists.
items.answer: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11

videos.answer: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11

source: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q1

items.question: Check if a triangle exists for each of the following set of lengths: (a) 1, 100, 100 (b) 3, 6, 9 (c) 1, 1, 5 (d) 5, 10, 12
steps: (a) The longest is 100 and 1 + 100 = 101 > 100: a triangle exists.
(b) The longest is 9 and 3 + 6 = 9, equal to 9: the circles touch, so no triangle.
(c) The longest is 5 and 1 + 1 = 2 < 5: no triangle.
(d) The longest is 12 and 5 + 10 = 15 > 12: a triangle exists.
items.answer: Triangles exist for (a) and (d); not for (b) (circles touch) or (c)

videos.answer: Triangles exist for (a) and (d); not for (b) (circles touch) or (c)

source: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q2

items.question: Does there exist an equilateral triangle with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does there exist an equilateral triangle of any sidelength? Justify your answer.
steps: For 50, 50, 50 the longest is 50 and the other two add to 50 + 50 = 100.
50 < 100, so the triangle inequality holds and an equilateral triangle exists.
For any side length s the other two add to s + s = 2s, and s < 2s as long as s is more than zero.
So the circles always cross: an equilateral triangle exists for every side length. It can be built with the two-arcs method of the first topic.
items.answer: Yes: 50 < 50 + 50, and in general s < s + s for any side length s above zero

videos.answer: Yes: 50 < 50 + 50, and in general s < s + s for any side length s above zero

source: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q3 (Try This)

items.question: For each of the following, give at least 5 possible values for the third length so there exists a triangle having these as sidelengths (decimal values could also be chosen): (a) 1, 100 (b) 5, 5 (c) 3, 7. See if you can describe all possible lengths of the third side in each case, so that a triangle exists with those sidelengths. For example, in case (a), all numbers strictly between 99 and 101 would be possible.
steps: The third length x must be less than the sum of the other two, and the other two lengths must each be less than the sum of x and the remaining length.
(a) 1 and 100: x < 1 + 100 = 101, and 100 < 1 + x gives x > 99. So x is strictly between 99 and 101: for example 99.5, 100, 100.5, 99.9 and 100.9.
(b) 5 and 5: x < 5 + 5 = 10, and 5 < 5 + x gives x > 0. So x is strictly between 0 and 10: for example 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
(c) 3 and 7: x < 3 + 7 = 10, and 7 < 3 + x gives x > 4. So x is strictly between 4 and 10: for example 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
In general, for two lengths p and q, the third length is strictly between the difference of p and q and the sum of p and q.
items.answer: (a) strictly between 99 and 101, for example 99.5, 100, 100.5; (b) strictly between 0 and 10, for example 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; (c) strictly between 4 and 10, for example 5, 6, 7, 8, 9

videos.answer: (a) strictly between 99 and 101, for example 99.5, 100, 100.5; (b) strictly between 0 and 10, for example 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; (c) strictly between 4 and 10, for example 5, 6, 7, 8, 9

source: A triangle has two sides of 6 cm and 5 cm that meet at a cor

items.question: A triangle has two sides of 6 cm and 5 cm that meet at a corner, and the angle at that corner is 30°. Is 30° the included angle? What if the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side?
steps: The two given sides, 6 cm and 5 cm, meet at one corner. The angle at that corner is between them, so 30° is the included angle.
If the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side, one of its arms would be the 6 cm side but the other arm would be a side that is not given.
That angle is not between the two given sides, so it is not the included angle. The measurements would then be a different kind of data.
items.answer: Yes, 30° is included when it sits between the 6 cm and 5 cm sides; at the other end it is not

videos.answer: Yes, 30° is included when it sits between the 6 cm and 5 cm sides; at the other end it is not

source: Construct a triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm and ∠A =

items.question: Construct a triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm and ∠A = 45°.
steps: Step 1: draw the base AB = 5 cm.
Step 2: place the protractor at A and mark 45° from AB. Draw a long arm through the mark.
Step 3: with the ruler or compass measure 4 cm from A along the arm and mark the point C.
Step 4: join BC.
Measuring BC gives about 3.6 cm, so the sides are 5 cm, 4 cm and about 3.6 cm.
items.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm, ∠A = 45° and BC about 3.6 cm

videos.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm, ∠A = 45° and BC about 3.6 cm

source: Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q1

items.question: Construct triangles for the following measurements where the angle is included between the sides: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm
steps: Use the same four steps each time: draw the first side as the base, make the angle at one end, mark the second side along the new arm, and join.
(a) AB = 3 cm, ∠A = 75°, AC = 7 cm. Joining BC gives a third side of about 6.9 cm.
(b) AB = 6 cm, ∠A = 25°, AC = 3 cm. The third side is about 3.5 cm, and the triangle is thin because the angle is small.
(c) AB = 3 cm, ∠A = 120°, AC = 8 cm. The angle is obtuse, and the third side is about 9.8 cm.
items.answer: (a) third side about 6.9 cm, (b) about 3.5 cm, (c) about 9.8 cm; all three triangles can be built

videos.answer: (a) third side about 6.9 cm, (b) about 3.5 cm, (c) about 9.8 cm; all three triangles can be built

source: Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q2

items.question: We have seen that triangles do not exist for all sets of sidelengths. Is there a combination of measurements in the case of two sides and the included angle where a triangle is not possible? Justify your answer using what you observe during construction.
steps: Draw the base and the arm for the angle, then mark the second side along the arm.
If the angle is 180° the arm points straight along the base, away from it, so the two sides lie on one line and joining the ends gives no triangle. Examples: 3 cm, 180°, 7 cm.

If the angle is more than 180°, for example 4 cm, 210°, 6 cm, the angle on the other side is less than 180° and the picture is the same as a smaller angle; a measure of 180° or more cannot be the angle of a triangle.
An angle of 0° puts the arm on top of the base, so there is no triangle either.
For every angle strictly between 0° and 180° the free ends can be joined, so a triangle always exists.
items.answer: Yes: no triangle when the included angle is 180° or more (for example 3 cm, 180°, 7 cm or 4 cm, 210°, 6 cm), or 0°; for any angle strictly between 0° and 180° a triangle exists

videos.answer: Yes: no triangle when the included angle is 180° or more (for example 3 cm, 180°, 7 cm or 4 cm, 210°, 6 cm), or 0°; for any angle strictly between 0° and 180° a triangle exists

source: Construct a triangle ABC where AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45° and ∠B =

items.question: Construct a triangle ABC where AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45° and ∠B = 80°.
steps: Step 1: draw the base AB = 5 cm. It is the side that both angles share, the included side.
Step 2: at A make an angle of 45° and draw a long arm. At B make an angle of 80° on the same side and draw a long arm.
Step 3: the two arms cross at C, the third vertex.
Measuring gives AC about 6.0 cm and BC about 4.3 cm, and the angle at C is 180° − 45° − 80° = 55°.
items.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45°, ∠B = 80°, AC about 6.0 cm, BC about 4.3 cm

videos.answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45°, ∠B = 80°, AC about 6.0 cm, BC about 4.3 cm

source: Figure it Out (two angles and the included side), Q1

items.question: Construct triangles for the following measurements: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75° (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60° (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°
steps: Draw the given side as the base. Make the first angle at one end and the second at the other end. The arms cross at the third vertex.
(a) 75° + 75° = 150° < 180°, so the arms cross; the third angle is 30° and the other two sides are each about 9.7 cm.
(b) 25° + 60° = 85° < 180°; the third angle is 95° and the other two sides are about 2.6 cm and 1.3 cm.
(c) 120° + 30° = 150° < 180°; the third angle is 30° and the other two sides are about 10.4 cm and 6 cm.
items.answer: All three triangles can be built: (a) third angle 30°, (b) third angle 95°, (c) third angle 30°

videos.answer: All three triangles can be built: (a) third angle 30°, (b) third angle 95°, (c) third angle 30°

source: Say why no triangle can be built from the angles 90°, 5 cm,

items.question: Say why no triangle can be built from the angles 90°, 5 cm, 90°, and from 100°, 5 cm, 95°.
steps: Draw the base of 5 cm.
With 90° at both ends the arms are straight up from the base, side by side. They never meet.
With 100° and 95° the arms lean outwards from the base, so they get further apart. They never meet.
Two angles that are each 90° or more always give arms that do not meet.
items.answer: No triangle: arms at 90° or more do not meet

videos.answer: No triangle: arms at 90° or more do not meet

source: The angle at A is 40°. Find the smallest angle at B for whic

items.question: The angle at A is 40°. Find the smallest angle at B for which the arms from A and B do not meet, and say whether the length AB matters.
steps: Draw AB and the arm from A at 40°. Call the line along this arm l.
The arm from B that does not meet l and leans the least is the line m parallel to l.
AB is a transversal of the parallel lines l and m. The angles on the same side add to 180°.
Any ∠B of 140° or more does not meet l; any ∠B less than 140° does. The length of AB is not used anywhere.
items.answer: ∠B = 140°: no triangle when ∠B is 140° or more; the length of AB does not matter

videos.answer: ∠B = 140°: no triangle when ∠B is 140° or more; the length of AB does not matter

source: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q1

items.question: For each of the following angles, find another angle for which a triangle is (a) possible, (b) not possible. Find at least two different angles for each category: (i) 30° (ii) 70° (iii) 54° (iv) 144°
steps: The other angle must be less than 180° minus the given angle; at that value or more the arms do not meet.
(i) 30°: possible if the other angle is less than 150°, for example 40° or 100°; not possible for 150° or more, for example 150° or 170°.
(ii) 70°: possible below 110°, for example 20° or 100°; not possible at 110° or more, for example 110° or 130°.
(iii) 54°: possible below 126°, for example 30° or 120°; not possible at 126° or more, for example 126° or 150°.
(iv) 144°: possible below 36°, for example 10° or 30°; not possible at 36° or more, for example 36° or 90°.
items.answer: (i) 30°: possible 40°, 100°; not possible 150°, 170°. (ii) 70°: possible 20°, 100°; not possible 110°, 130°. (iii) 54°: possible 30°, 120°; not possible 126°, 150°. (iv) 144°: possible 10°, 30°; not possible 36°, 90°

videos.answer: (i) 30°: possible 40°, 100°; not possible 150°, 170°. (ii) 70°: possible 20°, 100°; not possible 110°, 130°. (iii) 54°: possible 30°, 120°; not possible 126°, 150°. (iv) 144°: possible 10°, 30°; not possible 36°, 90°

source: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q2

items.question: Determine which of the following pairs can be the angles of a triangle and which cannot: (a) 35°, 150° (b) 70°, 30° (c) 90°, 85° (d) 50°, 150°
steps: Add the two angles. If the sum is less than 180° the arms meet; if it is 180° or more they do not.
(a) 35° + 150° = 185° is more than 180°: cannot.
(b) 70° + 30° = 100° is less than 180°: can.
(c) 90° + 85° = 175° is less than 180°: can.
(d) 50° + 150° = 200° is more than 180°: cannot.
items.answer: (b) and (c) can be the angles of a triangle; (a) and (d) cannot

videos.answer: (b) and (c) can be the angles of a triangle; (a) and (d) cannot

source: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q3

items.question: Like the triangle inequality, can you form a rule that describes the two angles for which a triangle is possible? Can the sum of the two angles be used for framing this rule?
steps: Take the pairs from the last question: the pairs that work, 70° and 30°, and 90° and 85°, add up to 100° and 175°. The pairs that fail add up to 185° and 200°.
For a first angle of 40° the second angle fails from 140° on, and 40° + 140° = 180°.
So the sum decides it: when the sum of the two angles is less than 180°, a triangle exists. When the sum is 180° or more, there is no triangle.
Each angle must also be more than 0°.
items.answer: A triangle exists when the two angles are each more than 0° and their sum is less than 180°; if the sum is 180° or more there is no triangle

videos.answer: A triangle exists when the two angles are each more than 0° and their sum is less than 180°; if the sum is 180° or more there is no triangle

source: Build a triangle with angles 60° and 70° at the ends of a ba

items.question: Build a triangle with angles 60° and 70° at the ends of a base of 5 cm, then one with a base of 7 cm, and compare the third angle.
steps: Base 5 cm: arms at 60° and 70° cross at C. The angle at C measures 50°.
Base 7 cm: arms at 60° and 70° cross at C. The angle at C still measures 50°.
The triangle with the longer base is a bigger copy, with every length scaled up but the same angles.
In both triangles 60° + 70° + 50° = 180°. The third angle is decided by the two given angles alone.
items.answer: The third angle is 50° for both bases; it does not depend on the length of the side

videos.answer: The third angle is 50° for both bases; it does not depend on the length of the side

source: In triangle ABC, ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°. Find ∠A using a line

items.question: In triangle ABC, ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°. Find ∠A using a line through A parallel to BC.
steps: Draw the line XY through A parallel to BC.
∠XAB and ∠B are alternate angles, so ∠XAB = 50°. ∠YAC and ∠C are alternate angles, so ∠YAC = 70°.
∠XAB, ∠BAC and ∠YAC together make the straight angle XAY: 50° + ∠BAC + 70° = 180°.
Construct to check: with 50° at B and 70° at C, the angle at A measures 60°.

source: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q1

items.question: Find the third angle of a triangle (using a parallel line) when two of the angles are: (a) 36°, 72° (b) 150°, 15° (c) 90°, 30° (d) 75°, 45°
steps: Draw a line through the third vertex parallel to the side between the two given angles; its two alternate angles are equal to the two given angles.
The third angle is what remains of 180°.

source: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q2

items.question: Can you construct a triangle all of whose angles are equal to 70°? If two of the angles are 70° what would the third angle be? If all the angles in a triangle have to be equal, then what must its measure be? Explore and find out.
steps: Three angles of 70° add up to 3 × 70° = 210°, which is more than 180°. So no triangle has all angles equal to 70°.
If two angles are 70°, the third is 180° − 70° − 70° = 40°.
If all three angles are equal and each is x, then 3x = 180°, so x = 60°.
items.answer: No triangle has three angles of 70°; two angles of 70° give a third of 40°; equal angles must each be 60°

videos.answer: No triangle has three angles of 70°; two angles of 70° give a third of 40°; equal angles must each be 60°

source: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q3 (Try This)

items.question: Here is a triangle in which we know ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Can you find ∠B and ∠C?
steps: The three angles add up to 180°, so ∠B + ∠C = 180° − 50° = 130°.
∠B and ∠C are equal, so each is half of 130°.

source: Prove that the three angles of a triangle ABC add up to 180°

items.question: Prove that the three angles of a triangle ABC add up to 180°, and check it with the paper fold.
steps: Draw a line XY through A parallel to BC.
Alternate angles give ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C.
∠XAB, ∠A and ∠YAC together make a straight angle: ∠XAB + ∠A + ∠YAC = 180°.
Replace ∠XAB by ∠B and ∠YAC by ∠C: ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
Paper fold: fold the three corners of a paper triangle in so that they meet at one point on the base. The three angles sit side by side along the straight base, which is 180°.
items.answer: ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° for every triangle

videos.answer: ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° for every triangle

source: Find ∠ACD, if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°, and then try ∠A = 35° a

items.question: Find ∠ACD, if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°, and then try ∠A = 35° and ∠B = 45°. What do you notice?
steps: First case: 50° + 60° + ∠ACB = 180°, so ∠ACB = 70°.
∠ACB and ∠ACD form a straight angle, so ∠ACD = 180° − 70° = 110°.
In the first case 110° = 50° + 60°; in the second case 80° = 35° + 45°.
The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.
items.answer: ∠ACD = 110°, and in general an exterior angle is the sum of the two opposite interior angles

videos.answer: ∠ACD = 110°, and in general an exterior angle is the sum of the two opposite interior angles

source: Draw the altitude from A to the base BC of a triangle ABC us

items.question: Draw the altitude from A to the base BC of a triangle ABC using a ruler and a set square.
steps: Step 1: keep the ruler along the base BC, and place the set square on the ruler with one edge of its right angle against the ruler.
Step 2: slide the set square along the ruler until its upright edge touches A.
Step 3: draw along the upright edge from A down to BC. This segment AD is the altitude.
AD is perpendicular to BC, so the angle at D is 90°, and the length of AD is the height of A from BC.
items.answer: AD, the perpendicular from A to BC, is the altitude from A; its length is the height

videos.answer: AD, the perpendicular from A to BC, is the altitude from A; its length is the height

source: In triangle ABC the angle at B is obtuse. Draw the altitude

items.question: In triangle ABC the angle at B is obtuse. Draw the altitude from A to BC and say where it lies.
steps: Extend the base BC beyond B into a longer line.
Slide the set square along the extended line until its upright edge touches A.
Draw the perpendicular from A to the extended line. The foot D is on the extension, outside the triangle.
So an altitude can lie outside the triangle.
Paper fold check: fold so that the base falls on itself with the crease through A. The two angles at the crease are equal and add up to 180°, so each is 90°.
items.answer: The altitude from A meets the extended base outside the triangle; the paper crease is perpendicular because its two equal angles add up to 180°

videos.answer: The altitude from A meets the extended base outside the triangle; the paper crease is perpendicular because its two equal angles add up to 180°

source: In a triangle ABC with a right angle at B, name two altitude

items.question: In a triangle ABC with a right angle at B, name two altitudes that are also sides.
steps: AB meets BC at 90°. The perpendicular from A to BC is AB itself, so AB is the altitude from A.
In the same way BC meets AB at 90°, so BC is the altitude from C to AB.
The altitude from B goes to the long side AC and lies inside the triangle.
items.answer: AB and BC are both sides and altitudes in a right-angled triangle with the right angle at B

videos.answer: AB and BC are both sides and altitudes in a right-angled triangle with the right angle at B

source: Name the kind of triangle with sides (a) 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (b

items.question: Name the kind of triangle with sides (a) 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (b) 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm (c) 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm, after checking each really is a triangle.
steps: Check each with the triangle inequality: 5 < 5 + 5; 8 < 5 + 5; 7 < 5 + 6. All three exist.
(a) All three sides are equal: equilateral.
(b) Exactly two sides are equal: isosceles.
(c) All three sides are different: scalene.
items.answer: (a) equilateral (b) isosceles (c) scalene

videos.answer: (a) equilateral (b) isosceles (c) scalene

source: Name the kind of triangle with angles (a) 50°, 60°, 70° (b)

items.question: Name the kind of triangle with angles (a) 50°, 60°, 70° (b) 90°, 50°, 40° (c) 120°, 30°, 30°. Which of them has at least one acute angle?
steps: (a) All three are acute: acute-angled.
(b) One angle is a right angle: right-angled.
(c) One angle is obtuse: obtuse-angled.
All three triangles have at least one acute angle, so having one acute angle does not tell the kind of triangle.
items.answer: (a) acute-angled (b) right-angled (c) obtuse-angled; all three have an acute angle

videos.answer: (a) acute-angled (b) right-angled (c) obtuse-angled; all three have an acute angle

items.question: Construct a triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct an altitude from A to BC.
steps: Check: 6 < 5 + 5, 5 < 5 + 6 and 5 < 6 + 5, so the triangle exists. Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles.
Draw BC = 5 cm. Draw an arc of radius 6 cm from B and an arc of radius 5 cm from C. They cross at A.
Slide the set square along BC until its upright edge touches A, and draw the perpendicular AD to BC.
Measure AD with the ruler: the altitude is about 4.8 cm.
items.answer: Isosceles triangle ABC; the altitude from A to BC measures about 4.8 cm

videos.answer: Isosceles triangle ABC; the altitude from A to BC measures about 4.8 cm

source: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q2

items.question: Construct a triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct an altitude from T to RY.
steps: Draw RY = 4 cm. At R make an angle of 140° and mark T at 7 cm along the arm. Join TY.
The angle at R is obtuse, so the altitude from T falls outside the triangle.
Extend YR beyond R. Slide the set square along it until its upright edge touches T, and draw the perpendicular TD to the extended line.
The angle TRD outside the triangle is 180° − 140° = 40°. Measure TD with the ruler: it is about 4.5 cm.
items.answer: The altitude from T meets YR extended beyond R; its length is about 4.5 cm

videos.answer: The altitude from T meets YR extended beyond R; its length is about 4.5 cm

source: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q3

items.question: Construct a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? Hint: the other measurements can take any values. Take AC as the base. What values can ∠A and ∠C take so that the other angle is 90°?
steps: Draw AC = 5 cm. The angle at B is 90°, so ∠A + ∠C = 90°.
Choose ∠A = 30°, then ∠C = 60°, and the arms cross at B. Choose ∠A = 45°, then ∠C = 45°. Choose ∠A = 70°, then ∠C = 20°. Each choice gives a different triangle.
∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90°, and ∠C is then 90° − ∠A.
There are infinitely many values to choose from, so there are infinitely many different triangles.
items.answer: Infinitely many: ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90° with ∠C = 90° − ∠A

videos.answer: Infinitely many: ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90° with ∠C = 90° − ∠A

source: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q4

items.question: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.
steps: Every equilateral triangle has three equal angles, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. No angle is 90° or more.
So an equilateral triangle can be neither right-angled nor obtuse-angled.
Isosceles right-angled: take a right angle with two equal sides, for example 4 cm and 4 cm. The other two angles are equal and add up to 90°, so each is 45°.
Isosceles obtuse-angled: take an angle of 120° between two equal sides of 5 cm. The other two angles are equal and add up to 60°, so each is 30°.
items.answer: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)

videos.answer: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)

source: A spider walks from one corner of a box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide

items.question: A spider walks from one corner of a box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high to the opposite corner, over two faces. Which path is shortest?
steps: Lay two faces flat side by side. The path is a straight line across the joined faces.
Case 1: the line goes 6 cm along and 4 + 3 = 7 cm across. Draw this rectangle and measure the diagonal: about 9.2 cm.
Case 2: 4 cm along and 6 + 3 = 9 cm across. The diagonal measures about 9.8 cm.
Case 3: 3 cm along and 6 + 4 = 10 cm across. The diagonal measures about 10.4 cm.
The shortest is the first, about 9.2 cm. It is shorter than going along the edges, which is 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 cm.
items.answer: About 9.2 cm, across the 6 by 4 face and the 6 by 3 face laid flat

videos.answer: About 9.2 cm, across the 6 by 4 face and the 6 by 3 face laid flat
